hook.title: 38 out of 60
hook.why: Scout looks great in demos. Priya has just run it against 60 real customer questions from Leo's queue, with a script that checks every answer, and it passed 38. Black Friday is three weeks away, and Maya wants a plan by tomorrow.
hook.stat: 60 test cases · 38 passed · 22 failed · 21 days to Black Friday
hook.narration: It's three weeks before Black Friday. Priya has just run Scout against sixty real questions from Leo's ticket queue, and a script checked every answer. Thirty-eight passed and twenty-two failed. Maya wants to buy a bigger model, and Priya wonders whether the checks are simply too strict. Before you open a single failure, what is your best guess about why Scout failed?

hook.prompt: Before anything is explained: why did Scout fail 22 of its 60 test cases?

hunches.label: The model isn't smart enough. Switch to a bigger, pricier one.
The tests are too strict. Many checks fail on harmless wording.
Most failures share one cause: Scout can't look orders up by email.

reveal.narration: Priya replays the run case by case. When a customer gives an order number, Scout calls get order and usually passes. But when a customer writes with only an email address, Scout has nowhere to put it. It passes the email as an order number, the tool returns an error, and Scout guesses. Fifteen of the twenty-two failures follow exactly that pattern. The model and the checks were fine; the tool was missing a way in.

steps.caption: Case 1: Where is ORB-10482? Scout calls get_order with the order number.
get_order finds the order. Right tool, right facts: the checker marks a pass.
Case 7: I ordered boots with grace@example.com, can I return them? No order number this time.
get_order only accepts an order_id, so Scout passes the email as one. Error: No order with ID grace@example.com.
With no order, Scout guesses: returns within 30 days are fine. Her boots arrived 62 days ago. Fail.
Priya sorts the 22 failures: 15 of them start with an email, not an order number, and every one hits the same error.
Final score: 38 of 60. The model and the checks were fine. get_order had no way to look orders up by email.

hook.wrap_correct: Right. Fifteen of the 22 failures share one cause: customers give an email, and get_order only accepted an order ID. One change to one tool clears most of the failures, no bigger model needed.
hook.wrap_wrong: Not quite. A bigger model would still have nowhere to put an email, and the checks were catching real mistakes. Fifteen of the 22 failures share one cause: get_order only took an order ID, so email-only customers hit an error and Scout guessed.
hook.wrap_point: Don't react to the score: read the failures, find the pattern they share, fix that one thing and measure again. That is how you build, test and evaluate an agent.

examples.title: Read the trace of a failing case
examples.intro: Priya reruns one failing case on its own, with the trace on, and walks it step by step.
examples.narration: Priya picks one failure: Grace, who wrote in with her email address and asked to return her boots. She runs that case alone with the trace on. Step one shows Scout calling get order, with Grace's email in the order number field. The tool returns an error, because no order has that ID. Step two shows Scout answering anyway, promising a return it never checked. The checker fails it, since the boots were delivered sixty-two days ago. The first bad step is step one: wrong arguments.

predict.stem: The trace has two steps, and both look wrong. Which is the first bad step?

options.text: Step 1: get_order is called with an email in the order_id field
Step 2: the reply gets the return window wrong
Neither: the checker is wrong about the 62 days

predict.rationale: Step 2 is wrong too, but it follows from step 1: with no order data, Scout had nothing to check the date against. Fix the first bad step and the later one usually fixes itself.

steps.caption: Case 7 failed in the full run. Priya reruns it on its own, with the trace on.
Trace step 1: get_order with order_id set to grace@example.com. An email in the order ID field.
Result: Error: No order with ID grace@example.com. The tool did its job; its input was wrong.
Trace step 2: no more tool calls. Scout replies anyway: unused items can be returned within 30 days.
Checker: no order was looked up, and the boots were delivered 62 days ago. FAIL.
First bad step: step 1, wrong arguments. The ignored error in step 2 follows from it.

examples.title: Fix the tool, not the model
examples.intro: One change to get_order and its description, then the same failing case again.
examples.narration: The fix belongs in the tool, not the model. Priya changes get order so it accepts either an order number or an email address. She updates the description too: pass the order number if the customer gives one, otherwise the email they ordered with. Then she reruns Grace's case. This time Scout calls get order with the email, and the tool finds her order: Ridge boots, delivered sixty-two days ago. Scout replies that the return window has closed and offers to pass her to the team. The checker marks it a pass.

predict.stem: What is the smallest change that fixes Grace's case?

options.text: Add a prompt rule: always ask the customer for their order number
Let get_order accept an email, and say so in its description
Switch to a bigger model so it guesses better

predict.rationale: Asking for the number adds a round trip for every customer who doesn't have it to hand, and a bigger model still has no way to search by email. The tool was the missing piece, and its description is how Scout learns to use it.

steps.caption: Priya fixes the tool, not the model: get_order now takes an order_id or an email.
The description changes too: pass order_id if the customer gives one, otherwise the email they ordered with.
Same case again: Grace writes in with her email and no order number.
Scout calls get_order with email grace@example.com. The tool finds ORB-10517 in orders.json.
The result: Ridge boots, $165, delivered 62 days ago. Now Scout has real facts to work with.
Scout replies: the 30-day window has closed, and offers to pass her to the team. Checker: PASS.

examples.title: Re-run the evaluation and read what's left
examples.intro: The same 60 cases and the same checks, with only get_order changed.
examples.narration: One case passing is not enough, so Priya re-runs all sixty. The fifteen email cases now pass. She checks the cases that passed before, and all thirty-eight still pass, so nothing broke. The score moves from thirty-eight to fifty-three, or eighty-eight percent. Then she reads the seven that still fail. Five are refunds over two hundred dollars where Scout tells the customer the money is on its way, though the tool said pending approval. Those are unsafe, so they are next.

predict.stem: The score jumps from 38 to 53. What should Priya check before celebrating?

options.text: That the score rose by more than 10 points
Nothing: a higher score means a better agent
That every case which passed before still passes, then what still fails

predict.rationale: A change can fix 15 cases and quietly break 3 others, and the total hides that. Compare case by case, then read the failures that are left: their kind matters more than their number.

steps.caption: One case passing isn't enough. Priya re-runs all 60 cases with the same checks; only get_order changed.
The 15 email cases now find their orders. All 15 pass.
She compares case by case: all 38 cases that passed before still pass. Nothing broke.
New score: 53 of 60, or 88 percent, up from 63 percent.

# Orbit Outdoor policies
## Returns
You can return any unused item within 30 days of delivery for a full refund. Items must be unused and in their original packaging.
## Return shipping
Return shipping is free on orders over $75. Under $75, a $6.95 return label is taken off the refund.
## Refunds
Refunds go back to the original payment method within 5 business days of the return arriving. Refunds over $200 must be approved by a member of the support team.
## Exchanges
Exchanging for a different size is free if the new size is in stock.
## Shipping
Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days. Express takes 1 to 2 business days.
## Damaged items
Send a photo within 7 days of delivery and we send a replacement or a full refund.

# prompts.py: Scout's system prompt (one job, clear limits)
SCOUT_SYSTEM = """You are Scout, the support assistant for Orbit Outdoor, an online shop for hiking, camping and climbing gear.

Your job: answer customers' questions about their orders, returns, exchanges and refunds. Nothing else.

How you work:
- Plan before you act: decide which facts you need, then use your tools to get them.
- Look up an order with get_order before you say anything about it. Customers may give an order ID or the email they ordered with.
- Answer every policy question from search_policy results, never from memory.
- Check stock with check_stock before you offer an exchange.
- If a tool returns an error, tell the customer you can't check that right now. Never guess a status, date or amount.
- Refunds: use request_refund. If it returns pending_approval, tell the customer a member of the support team will review it. Never say a refund is approved unless the tool says so.
- If the customer asks for a person, is upset, or needs something you can't do (like product advice), use hand_off with a short summary and tell them a member of the support team will reply.
- If asked for something unrelated to Orbit orders (like writing a poem), say you can only help with orders, returns, exchanges and refunds.

Style: warm, plain and short, two to four sentences. Use the customer's first name when you know it."""

steps.check: `python -c "from prompts import SCOUT_SYSTEM; print(SCOUT_SYSTEM[:40])"` prints `You are Scout, the support assistant for`.
steps.tip: Keep the tool names in the prompt exactly as they appear in **tools.py**. If you ever rename a tool, rename it in both places.

steps.title: Assemble the loop with a trace
steps.body: agent.py brings it all together: the tool loop with its step limit from Module 3, the memory, and a trace line for every tool call and result. run_agent returns the reply and the list of tools Scout used, which is exactly what the tests will check.
actions: Open **agent.py** and replace everything in it with the code below.
Find the three new parts: the trace `print` lines, `remember`, which pins the name and order ID once `get_order` finds the order, and the `return reply, tools_used` at the end of `run_agent`.
Run `python agent.py` and ask `Where is my order ORB-10482?`

# agent.py: Scout's loop, with a trace of every step and memory across turns
import json

import anthropic

from memory import Conversation
from prompts import SCOUT_SYSTEM
from tools import TOOLS, run_tool

client = anthropic.Anthropic()            # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"
MAX_STEPS = 6


def short(text, limit=120):
    """One line, cut short, so the trace stays readable."""
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    return text if len(text) <= limit else text[:limit] + "..."


def remember(tool_name, output, convo):
    """Once get_order finds an order, pin the customer's name and order ID."""
    if tool_name == "get_order" and not output.startswith("Error"):
        data = json.loads(output)
        order = data["orders"][0] if "orders" in data else data
        convo.pin("name", order["customer"])
        convo.pin("order_id", order["order_id"])


def run_agent(question, convo=None, verbose=True):
    """Answer one customer message. Returns Scout's reply and the tools it used."""
    if convo is None:
        convo = Conversation()            # a fresh chat, e.g. for each test case
    convo.add_user(question)              # pins any order ID, email or name
    system = convo.system_prompt(SCOUT_SYSTEM)
    messages = list(convo.messages)       # a copy: this run's tool calls stay out of memory
    tools_used = []

    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):         # always a step limit
        response = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000,
                                          system=system, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            break
        results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                tools_used.append(block.name)
                if verbose:
                    print(f"[{step + 1}] {block.name} {json.dumps(block.input)}")
                try:
                    output = run_tool(block.name, block.input)
                    results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": output})
                except Exception as err:
                    output = f"Error: {err}"
                    results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                    "content": output, "is_error": True})
                if verbose:
                    print(f"    -> {short(output)}")
                remember(block.name, output, convo)
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # all results in one message

    if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":    # out of steps in the middle of the job
        reply = "Sorry, I couldn't finish that. A member of our support team will pick it up."
    else:
        reply = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    convo.add_assistant(reply)
    return reply, tools_used


if __name__ == "__main__":
    convo = Conversation()
    print("Scout is ready. Type quit to stop.")
    while True:
        question = input("\nYou: ").strip()
        if question.lower() in ("quit", "exit"):
            break
        if question:
            reply, tools_used = run_agent(question, convo)
            print(f"\nScout: {reply}")

steps.title: Write evaluate.py and get your first score
steps.body: evaluate.py runs every case through run_agent with a fresh memory, applies the checks, prints PASS or FAIL for each case and the pass rate, and adds the score to tests/scores.txt so you can track it over time.

values.value:
# evaluate.py: run every test case through Scout, check it, print a pass rate
import json
import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from agent import run_agent

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
cases = json.loads((HERE / "tests" / "cases.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
note = " ".join(sys.argv[1:]) or "no note"       # e.g. python evaluate.py "first run"
passed = 0

for case in cases:
    reply, tools_used = run_agent(case["question"], verbose=False)   # fresh memory per case
    text = reply.lower()
    problems = []
    expected = case["expected_tool"]
    if expected and expected not in tools_used:                       # right tool?
        problems.append(f"expected {expected}, called {tools_used or 'no tools'}")
    for fact in case["must_include"]:                                 # key facts in the reply?
        if fact.lower() not in text:
            problems.append(f"missing '{fact}'")
    for bad in case.get("must_not_include", []):                      # nothing invented or promised?
        if bad.lower() in text:
            problems.append(f"should not say '{bad}'")
    if problems:
        print(f"FAIL  {case['id']}: {'; '.join(problems)}")
        print(f"      reply: {' '.join(reply.split())[:160]}")
    else:
        passed += 1
        print(f"PASS  {case['id']}")

rate = round(100 * passed / len(cases))
print(f"\n{passed} of {len(cases)} passed ({rate}%)")
with open(HERE / "tests" / "scores.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:   # keep a score history
    log.write(f"{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}  {passed}/{len(cases)}  {rate}%  {note}\n")

steps.check: Twelve PASS or FAIL lines appear, then a summary such as `11 of 12 passed (92%)`. **tests/scores.txt** now has one line with the date, the score and your note. Your score may differ by a case or so from run to run.
steps.tip: A failure isn't always Scout's fault. If the reply is right but worded differently, for example Thu instead of Thursday, fix the check. If the facts are wrong, it's a real bug.

steps.title: Break it on purpose, then measure again
steps.body: A test set earns its keep by catching what a change breaks. Recreate the bug from this module's opening, an order lookup that can't take an email, and watch the score catch it.
actions: In **tools.py**, inside get_order's `input_schema`, put `#` at the start of the line that begins `"email":`.
In the same tool, replace the three-line `"description"` with the single line below, so it no longer mentions email.
Run `python evaluate.py "no email lookup"` and look at the track-email case.
Undo both changes, run `python evaluate.py "email lookup back"`, then open **tests/scores.txt** and compare the three lines.

values.label: Temporary get_order description
values.value: "description": "Look up an Orbit order by its ID (like ORB-10482). Returns status, items, carrier and tracking number.",

steps.check: With email lookup gone, track-email should fail: Scout can't find Ana's order from her email, so Thursday never reaches the reply. After the undo, the score comes back, and **scores.txt** shows the dip and the recovery. If track-email still passes, run its question in `python agent.py` and read the trace to see how Scout got around the change.
steps.tip: Always write a short note with each run. A week from now, the notes in scores.txt are how you'll know which change moved the score.

finish.title: Scout is assembled and measured
finish.body: The whole project now lives in one folder: six tools on fake data, a loop with a step limit and a trace, memory with pinned facts, twelve test cases and a score history. In Module 6 you'll add guardrails, put Scout behind an API and keep an eye on what it costs.
checklist: data/orders.json holds the five sample orders, and tools.py has all six tools
python agent.py prints a trace line for every tool call and its result
Scout answers a follow-up question from its pinned facts
tests/cases.json has at least 10 cases, and evaluate.py prints a pass rate
tests/scores.txt shows the dip when you broke email lookup, and the recovery

lab.title: Ship it or fix it?
lab.intro: Three reports land on your desk in launch week. For each one, decide whether Scout ships, or what has to change first.

scenarios.title: 92 percent, and a pattern
scenarios.situation: Priya tried a prompt change to make Scout's replies warmer. The new run scores 55 of 60, 92 percent, above Maya's 90 percent target, and Leo is ready to switch Scout on. You open the five failures and one trace behind them.

context.label: evaluate.py output and one trace
lines: reply: Great news! Your $240 refund is approved.
reply: All done, Owen! Your $310 refund has been approved.
FAIL  refund-265, refund-410, refund-299: same pattern

options.text: Not yet. The tool said pending_approval and Scout ignored it: fix the refund replies, re-run, then ship.
options.why: Every failure is the same unsafe one: money promised without the approval the policy requires. The trace shows an ignored tool result, so the fix is clear, and it must land before launch.

options.text: Ship it. 92 percent beats the target, and five failures in sixty is normal.
options.why: The score is an average, and it hides what failed. Five customers told their big refund is approved, when a person hasn't approved it, is a policy break and a money problem.

options.text: Hold it and switch to a bigger model, since this one is clearly confused.
options.why: The trace shows a specific bug, an ignored tool result after a prompt change. A bigger model costs more and may make the same mistake; fix the instruction and re-run.

hints: Look at what the five failures have in common, not at how many there are.
Compare what request_refund returned with what Scout told the customer.
scenarios.debrief: A pass rate is an average, and averages hide what failed. Here every failure is the same unsafe one, and the trace pins it down: the tool said pending_approval and the warmer prompt made Scout gloss over it. Fix the refund replies, re-run the full set, and ship when the failures left are harmless.

scenarios.title: 85 percent, and a little stiff
scenarios.situation: A week later, Orbit's test set includes tone checks: use the customer's name, greet them, stay under 80 words. A new run scores 51 of 60, 85 percent. Every tool and fact check passes; all nine failures are tone. Launch is in two days.

context.label: evaluate.py output
lines: FAIL  track-id: tone: no greeting, reads like a form
reply: Order ORB-10482. Status: shipped. Expected: Thursday.
FAIL  exchange: tone: customer's name not used
reply: The medium is in stock. Size exchanges are free.
... 6 more FAIL lines, all tone checks
Right tool: 60 of 60 · Key facts: 60 of 60 · Policy kept: 60 of 60

options.text: Hold the launch until every tone check passes.
options.why: These failures hurt no one: the facts and the policy are right in every case. Holding the launch leaves Leo's team drowning in tickets over replies that are merely stiff.

options.text: Ship, with Leo's team reviewing a sample of chats in the first weeks, and polish the tone next.
options.why: Tools, facts and policy are at 60 of 60, so every failure left is safe. Monitoring catches what the test set can't, and tone is a good next change to measure.

options.text: Switch to a bigger model before launch to fix the wording.
options.why: It costs more on every chat, and you would have to re-run and re-check everything two days before launch, for a problem a prompt tweak can fix afterwards.

hints: Did any failure give a customer a wrong fact or break a policy?
Who is actually harmed by Status: shipped. Expected: Thursday?
scenarios.debrief: Good enough means the failures left are safe. The tone checks are worth keeping, but they measure polish, not safety, and the checks that protect customers are all passing. Ship with people watching real chats, make tone the next measured change, and keep the score history going.

scenarios.title: Just one more job
scenarios.situation: Two weeks before launch, Maya messages you. She loves Scout and wants it to write Orbit's Black Friday marketing emails too. It already knows the products and the customers, so why not?

context.label: Message from Maya
lines: maya, 9:12 AM: scout is brilliant. can it also write our black friday marketing emails?
maya, 9:13 AM: it already knows our products and our customers
maya, 9:13 AM: it's just one more tool, right? launch is in two weeks

options.text: Add a write_marketing_email tool now. It's one tool, and Scout already has the data.
options.why: It's a different job with different readers, risks and success measures. It adds a tool Scout can pick by mistake in support chats, and none of the 60 tests cover it, two weeks before launch.

options.text: Add it to the system prompt instead of as a tool, so the tests don't change.
options.why: The job still grows; you've just hidden it from the tests. Scout would now do something nobody measures, inside the support agent customers talk to.

options.text: Keep Scout to its one job for launch, and scope marketing emails as a separate project afterwards.
options.why: Scout's scope, tests and targets are all built around support. A new job deserves its own scoping, its own test set and its own decision about whether it even needs an agent.

hints: Go back to Scout's scope: what is its one job?
What would you have to add to the test set if Scout took this on?
scenarios.debrief: Scope is a decision you defend, not a wish list. A support agent and a marketing writer have different users, risks and measures of success. Say yes to the idea and no to the timing: finish the one job well, then scope the next one properly, starting with whether it needs an agent at all.

variants.title: Health check · Scout
variants.stem: Priya tweaks Scout's system prompt so replies are shorter. Before she keeps the change, what should she do?

options.text: Run the full test set and compare the score and the failing cases with the last run
Try three questions by hand, and keep it if the replies look shorter
Nothing: a prompt change can't affect which tools Scout calls

variants.rationale: Any change can fix one thing and break another, and prompt changes often affect tool choice too. Re-running the same test set after every change, and comparing which cases moved, is how you find out.

variants.title: Trace reading · Scout
variants.stem: A customer asks if the Storm jacket comes in medium. The trace: check_stock with sku 'Storm jacket medium', then Error: Unknown SKU. Scout replies: Yes, it's in stock! What went wrong first?

options.text: Wrong tool: Scout should have called search_policy
Wrong arguments: Scout passed a product name where the tool needs a SKU
A loop: Scout called check_stock too many times

variants.rationale: The first bad step is the input: a product name instead of a SKU like JKT-STORM-M. Showing the SKU format in the tool description fixes it. The cheerful reply is a second bug, an ignored error, which the never-guess rule in the prompt should catch.

variants.title: Growing Scout · cancellations
variants.stem: Orbit wants Scout to cancel orders that haven't shipped yet, and you've written a cancel_order tool. What is the best way to add it?

options.text: Add cancel_order together with the other features on the wish list, then test everything at the end
Add the tool and test only the new cancel questions, since nothing else changed
Add the tool, read the traces for a few cancel questions, add cancel cases to the test set, then re-run the full evaluation

variants.rationale: One piece at a time, run after each change, and measure against the whole test set: a new tool can change how Scout chooses between the old ones. Cancelling is also an action that changes an order, so it needs the same care as refunds.
